notes.front: What are the NIMS Management Characteristics?
notes.back: Fourteen characteristics that are the foundation of all NIMS command and coordination, including ICS.
notes.explanation: Everything else in this topic is one of these fourteen; knowing the umbrella term first makes each one easier to place.
notes.example: Like fourteen ingredients that, together, make ICS work: common terminology, modular organization, span of control, and so on.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 4, SM-p47; "formerly called ICS Management Characteristics", NIMS 2017 Instructor/Student Learning Materials, p20

notes.front: What does Common Terminology give ICS?
notes.back: Standard names for organizational functions, resource descriptions and incident facilities, so different organizations can work together.
notes.explanation: Without it, "Engine 3" or "Code 3" mean different things to different agencies at the same incident.
notes.example: Like every agency agreeing to call the same radio channel "Tac 1", instead of each using its own name for it.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 5, SM-p48

notes.front: What is Plain Language, for NIMS purposes?
notes.back: Communication the intended audience can understand: avoiding or limiting codes, abbreviations and jargon in incidents involving more than one agency.
notes.explanation: It is the practical rule behind Common Terminology: say it so every agency on the incident understands it.
notes.example: Like saying "structure fire" instead of a department-specific radio code number.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What is Clear Text?
notes.back: Communication that does not use codes.
notes.explanation: It is the narrower cousin of Plain Language: no codes at all, rather than just limiting jargon.
notes.example: Like saying "officer down" over the radio instead of a coded distress signal.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What does Modular Organization mean in ICS?
notes.back: The ICS organizational structure develops top-down in a modular fashion, based on the incident’s size, complexity and hazards.
notes.explanation: It explains why a small incident has almost no structure while a huge one grows a full General Staff — the same system just expands.
notes.example: Like a telescope: it extends only as far as the incident actually needs.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 7, SM-p50

notes.front: What does Management by Objectives (MBO) include?
notes.back: Setting specific, measurable objectives; identifying strategies, tactics and tasks; issuing assignments and plans; and documenting results.
notes.explanation: It is the reasoning method behind every Incident Action Plan: objectives first, then how to reach them.
notes.example: Like setting "clear the eastern block by 6pm" before deciding which crews do it and how.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 8, SM-p51

notes.front: What is Incident Action Planning?
notes.back: The process that guides incident management activities, producing an Incident Action Plan that captures priorities, objectives, strategies and assignments for an operational period.
notes.explanation: It is the process; the Incident Action Plan (next card) is its product.
notes.example: Like the meeting and drafting process behind tomorrow’s shift plan, not the printed plan itself.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 9, SM-p52

notes.front: What is an Incident Action Plan (IAP)?
notes.back: An oral or written plan with the objectives of the Incident Commander or Unified Command, addressing tactics and support for one operational period.
notes.explanation: It is the single document (or spoken plan) every section works from during that period.
notes.example: Like a shift briefing sheet: who is doing what, with what resources, for the next 12 hours.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What is an Operational Period?
notes.back: The time scheduled for executing a set of operations actions, as specified in the IAP; typically 12 to 24 hours.
notes.explanation: Every IAP is written for one Operational Period, so the two terms are almost always used together.
notes.example: Like a single work shift the IAP is written to cover.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What is Span of Control?
notes.back: The number of subordinates for which a supervisor is responsible, usually expressed as a ratio of supervisors to individuals.
notes.explanation: ICS grows or shrinks its structure specifically to keep this ratio manageable.
notes.example: Like one team lead overseeing five workers, rather than fifteen.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What does Incident Facilities and Locations cover?
notes.back: Support facilities set up for specific purposes, such as the Incident Command Post, incident base, staging areas, camps, casualty triage areas, and shelters.
notes.explanation: Knowing these named locations lets responders find the right place for the right task.
notes.example: Like knowing the Staging Area is where you wait, not the Incident Command Post where decisions are made.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 13, SM-p57

notes.front: What is Comprehensive Resource Management?
notes.back: Standard mechanisms to identify, order, mobilize, track, demobilize, and reimburse and restock resources such as personnel, teams and equipment.
notes.explanation: It covers a resource’s whole life cycle at an incident, not just its arrival.
notes.example: Like tracking an ambulance from the moment it is ordered to the moment it is released and reimbursed.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 14, SM-p58

notes.front: What are Resources, in NIMS terms?
notes.back: Personnel, equipment, teams, supplies and facilities available or potentially available for assignment, described by kind and type.
notes.explanation: Every later card about typing, ordering or tracking resources builds on this definition.
notes.example: Like an ambulance crew: personnel and equipment together, described by what kind and type they are.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What are Integrated Communications?
notes.back: A common communications plan and interoperable processes and systems, including voice and data links, to maintain connectivity, situational awareness and information sharing.
notes.explanation: This is the mechanism, not just the "plain language" rule, that lets agencies actually talk to each other.
notes.example: Like every agency’s radios being programmed to a shared channel for the incident.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 16, SM-p60

notes.front: What does Establishment and Transfer of Command require?
notes.back: Command must be clearly established at the start; a transfer always includes a briefing for the incoming commander and is announced to all personnel.
notes.explanation: It sets the ground rule that a later topic’s detailed transfer procedure builds on.
notes.example: Like the very first arriving officer declaring "I have command," so no one is left guessing who is in charge.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 18, SM-p62

notes.front: What is Unified Command?
notes.back: An ICS application for incidents with more than one agency having jurisdiction, with no single commander, only jointly approved objectives.
notes.explanation: It solves the problem of multiple agencies each having legitimate authority over the same incident.
notes.example: Like a fire chief and a police chief jointly approving one set of objectives for the same event.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 20, SM-p64

notes.front: What is Chain of Command?
notes.back: The orderly line of authority within the ranks of incident management organizations.
notes.explanation: It describes the overall hierarchy; Unity of Command (next) describes each person’s single link within it.
notes.example: Like a company’s org chart: authority flows down one defined line.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What is Unity of Command?
notes.back: Each individual involved in incident management reports to and takes direction from only one person.
notes.explanation: It is the individual-level rule inside the broader Chain of Command hierarchy.
notes.example: Like a firefighter taking orders only from their assigned ICS supervisor, not from two bosses at once.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What principles make up Accountability in ICS?
notes.back: Check-in/check-out, incident action planning, unity of command, personal responsibility, span of control, and resource tracking.
notes.explanation: It groups several other characteristics under one heading: together they let ICS answer "who is doing what, and who is responsible."
notes.example: Like a warehouse that logs every item in and out, so nothing is lost track of.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 23, SM-p67

notes.front: What is Check-In?
notes.back: The process through which resources first report to an incident; all responders report in to receive an assignment.
notes.explanation: It is the very first accountability step for anyone arriving at an incident.
notes.example: Like signing in at a job site before starting your shift.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What does the Dispatch/Deployment characteristic require?
notes.back: Resources deploy only when requested or dispatched by an appropriate authority; unrequested resources should not self-dispatch.
notes.explanation: It exists to stop an incident being overwhelmed by well-meaning but unrequested help.
notes.example: Like an off-duty responder waiting to be called rather than driving straight to the scene.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 24, SM-p68

notes.front: What is Dispatch, in NIMS terms?
notes.back: The ordered movement of a resource to an assigned operational mission, or an administrative move between locations.
notes.explanation: It is the specific act the Dispatch/Deployment rule is protecting: an ordered, not a self-initiated, movement.
notes.example: Like a fire engine being ordered to a specific address, rather than driving there on its own initiative.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What is Information and Intelligence Management?
notes.back: Established processes for gathering, analyzing, assessing, sharing and managing incident information and intelligence.
notes.explanation: It is the last of the 14 characteristics, and the one that later topics build a whole function around.
notes.example: Like a Planning Section keeping one shared, verified picture of the incident instead of scattered rumors.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 27, SM-p71

notes.front: What are Essential Elements of Information (EEI)?
notes.back: Important and standard information items that support timely and informed decisions.
notes.explanation: They are the specific facts Information and Intelligence Management is set up to gather.
notes.example: Like "how many people are still inside the building" during a structure fire.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What should responders avoid using on the radio during an incident?
notes.back: Radio codes, agency-specific codes, acronyms or jargon — they can cause confusion or compromise life safety.
notes.explanation: This is the practical instruction Common Terminology and Plain Language exist to enforce.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 5, SM-p48

notes.front: When must an Incident Action Plan be written rather than oral?
notes.back: For smaller or less complex incidents an IAP may be oral or written, except hazardous-materials incidents, which always require a written IAP.
notes.explanation: This is the one incident type where "oral is fine" never applies.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 9, SM-p52

notes.front: Besides hazmat, when does a written IAP become increasingly important?
notes.back: When the incident is likely to run past one operational period, grows more complex, or involves multiple jurisdictions or agencies.
notes.explanation: These are the practical triggers for moving from an oral plan to a written one.
notes.source: IS-0700.b Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 6, p71 (also IS-0200.c SM Lesson 1)

notes.front: Which of the four questions every IAP must answer is about the goal itself?
notes.back: "What do we want to do?"
notes.explanation: Every IAP, oral or written, must answer all four; this is one of the four.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 9, SM-p53

notes.front: Which of the four questions every IAP must answer is about responsibility?
notes.back: "Who is responsible for doing it?"
notes.explanation: Every IAP, oral or written, must answer all four; this is one of the four.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 9, SM-p53

notes.front: Which of the four questions every IAP must answer is about coordination?
notes.back: "How do we communicate with each other?"
notes.explanation: Every IAP, oral or written, must answer all four; this is one of the four.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 9, SM-p53

notes.front: Which of the four questions every IAP must answer is about safety?
notes.back: "What is the procedure if someone is injured?"
notes.explanation: Every IAP, oral or written, must answer all four; this is one of the four.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 9, SM-p53

notes.front: What is the optimal Span of Control ratio, as a guideline?
notes.back: One supervisor to five subordinates (1:5) — a guideline, not a fixed rule.
notes.explanation: Incident personnel use judgement to vary this ratio; it is a starting point, not a limit.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 11, SM-p55

notes.front: Which span-of-control factor is about the kind of incident, not the number of people?
notes.back: The type of incident.
notes.explanation: Any of these four factors can push the ratio away from the 1:5 guideline.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 11, SM-p55

notes.front: Which span-of-control factor is about how demanding the task itself is?
notes.back: The nature of the task.
notes.explanation: Any of these four factors can push the ratio away from the 1:5 guideline.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 11, SM-p55

notes.front: Which span-of-control factor covers danger and safety conditions at the incident?
notes.back: Hazards and safety factors.
notes.explanation: Any of these four factors can push the ratio away from the 1:5 guideline.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 11, SM-p55

notes.front: Which span-of-control factor is about how far apart crews and equipment are?
notes.back: Distances between personnel and resources.
notes.explanation: Any of these four factors can push the ratio away from the 1:5 guideline.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 11, SM-p55

notes.front: Once assigned to an incident, who do you report to?
notes.back: Only your ICS supervisor — not your day-to-day supervisor.
notes.explanation: This is Unity of Command applied to a specific, easily-forgotten situation.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 22, SM-p66

notes.front: What makes an IAP effective, beyond stating objectives?
notes.back: Covering a set timeframe; being proactive; stating activities; assigning responsibilities; identifying resources; and specifying communication protocols.
notes.explanation: These are the features IS-100.c lists beyond just "set objectives".
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 9, SM-p52

notes.front: What should your initial briefing after Check-In cover?
notes.back: The situation, your job, your coworkers, your work area, break areas, how to get resources, operational periods, and safety procedures/PPE.
notes.explanation: This is what a new arrival should expect once checked in and assigned an ICS supervisor.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 24 note, SM-p68

notes.front: What does "intelligence" mean in NIMS, specifically?
notes.back: Exclusively threat-related information developed by law enforcement, medical surveillance and other investigative organizations.
notes.explanation: This is narrower than the everyday sense of "intelligence" — it excludes general situational information.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 27, SM-p71

notes.front: A responder says the 14 NIMS Management Characteristics are unique to ICS and do not apply to EOCs. Is that right?
notes.back: No — they are the foundation of all NIMS command and coordination, including but not limited to ICS.
notes.explanation: They apply across ICS, EOCs and the other Command and Coordination structures, not to ICS alone.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 4, SM-p46

notes.front: Two mutual-aid crews each use their own department’s radio code for "all clear," and one crew nearly re-enters a hazard zone. What ICS characteristic was missing?
notes.back: Common Terminology — shared, standard names and terms across organizations.
notes.explanation: This is a direct, concrete failure of the characteristic, not just an abstract definition.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 5, SM-p47

notes.front: A dispatcher uses a local ten-code over a multi-agency channel during a hazmat response. Does this follow the Common Terminology rule?
notes.back: No — organizations should avoid radio codes, agency-specific codes and jargon during an incident.
notes.explanation: This applies the abstract rule to a specific radio call.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 5, SM-p48

notes.front: A dispatcher considers using an agency-specific acronym on a multi-agency channel. What should they use instead?
notes.back: Plain language: wording the intended audience across every agency can understand.
notes.explanation: This distinguishes Plain Language, the general communication style, from the specific "no codes" instruction.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: A structure fire grows from one engine company to a multi-branch operation over two hours. Who is responsible for expanding the ICS organization to match it?
notes.back: The Incident Commander — responsible for establishing and expanding the modular organization.
notes.explanation: This shows Modular Organization is not automatic — someone has to actively build it as the incident grows.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 7, SM-p50
notes.choices:
A) The Incident Commander
B) Whichever Section Chief arrives first
C) The dispatch center
notes.choicesExplained: B: no Section Chiefs exist yet at a one-engine incident; positions are only created as the Incident Commander delegates them. C: dispatch sends resources but does not build the ICS organization.

notes.front: A Section Chief starts assigning tasks before the Incident Commander has set any objectives. What step of Management by Objectives has been skipped?
notes.back: Establishing specific, measurable objectives — the first step, which should come before tasks are assigned.
notes.explanation: MBO is a sequence; skipping the first step leaves later steps with nothing to aim at.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 8, SM-p51

notes.front: A team is debating strategies and tactics for the next 12 hours but has not yet written anything down. Which process are they in the middle of?
notes.back: Incident Action Planning — the process that produces the IAP.
notes.explanation: This distinguishes the process (planning) from its product (the plan itself).
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 9, SM-p52

notes.front: A small, single-agency incident is resolved using only a spoken plan the Incident Commander gives to two responders. Is this still an IAP?
notes.back: Yes — an IAP may be oral, not only written, for smaller or less complex incidents.
notes.explanation: This tests that "IAP" does not mean only the printed ICS form.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: A hazmat incident commander plans to brief the team verbally instead of using a written IAP, to save time. Is this allowed?
notes.back: No — hazardous-materials incidents always require a written IAP.
notes.explanation: This is the one firm exception to the "oral is fine for small incidents" rule.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 9, SM-p52
notes.choices:
A) No, hazmat always requires a written IAP
B) Yes, if the incident is small
C) Yes, if all responders already know the plan
notes.choicesExplained: B: incident size does not create an exception for hazmat. C: familiarity does not satisfy the written-IAP requirement for hazmat.

notes.front: A written IAP lists objectives and assignments but never says what to do if someone is hurt. What is missing?
notes.back: An answer to one of the four required IAP questions: the injury procedure.
notes.explanation: Even a well-written IAP fails this specific completeness test if it skips one of the four questions.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 9, SM-p53

notes.front: A wildfire response plans in 12-hour blocks, each with its own set of objectives. What is each block called?
notes.back: An Operational Period.
notes.explanation: This links the abstract definition to the everyday practice of planning incident work in blocks.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: One supervisor is trying to directly oversee fifteen individual responders during a fast-moving incident. What ICS characteristic does this strain?
notes.back: Span of Control — the ratio has grown well past the 1:5 guideline.
notes.explanation: This connects the abstract ratio to a recognisable overload situation.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: A supervisor manages exactly seven subordinates during a low-hazard, simple task. Does this automatically break the ICS Span of Control guideline?
notes.back: No — 1:5 is a guideline, not a fixed rule; personnel use judgement for the actual incident conditions.
notes.explanation: This tests that the ratio is advisory, not a hard limit.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 11, SM-p55

notes.front: A Division Supervisor manages a hazardous, spread-out incident with only three crews, yet still feels overloaded. Which factors explain that, despite the low headcount?
notes.back: Hazards/safety factors and the distances between personnel and resources.
notes.explanation: This shows the four factors, not just headcount, determine a manageable span.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 11, SM-p55

notes.front: Responders need somewhere to wait, ready, until they are given a task. Which incident facility is that?
notes.back: A Staging Area.
notes.explanation: This links the general list of facilities to the specific one used for waiting resources.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 13, SM-p57

notes.front: A Logistics team orders new radios, then loses track of who has them once the incident ends. What part of Comprehensive Resource Management failed?
notes.back: Tracking, and then demobilizing: the radios were not tracked through to their release.
notes.explanation: This tests the full life-cycle scope of the characteristic, not just ordering.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 14, SM-p58

notes.front: Is a single fire engine, on its own with no crew, a "Resource" under NIMS?
notes.back: Yes — equipment on its own is a Resource, as are personnel, teams, supplies and facilities.
notes.explanation: Resources is a broad category: any one of these five kinds counts on its own, not just combinations of them.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: Two agencies’ radios cannot reach the same channel during a joint response. What ICS characteristic addresses this directly?
notes.back: Integrated Communications — a common plan and interoperable systems for voice and data.
notes.explanation: This is the mechanism, distinct from Common Terminology, which is about the words used rather than the equipment.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 16, SM-p60

notes.front: No one at a fast-moving incident has clearly said who is in command. What ICS characteristic is being violated?
notes.back: Establishment and Transfer of Command — command must be clearly established at the start.
notes.explanation: This is the failure mode the characteristic is designed to prevent.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 18, SM-p62

notes.front: A wildfire crosses from a county’s jurisdiction into a neighboring state park’s jurisdiction, and both agencies have legal authority over their part of it. What ICS application fits this best?
notes.back: Unified Command — both agencies jointly approve objectives without one commanding the other.
notes.explanation: This tests recognising the situation (multiple legitimate jurisdictions) that calls for Unified Command.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary
notes.choices:
A) Unified Command
B) One agency simply takes over the other’s jurisdiction
C) Two separate, uncoordinated Incident Commanders
notes.choicesExplained: B: neither agency’s authority is removed under NIMS; jurisdiction is not overridden. C: uncoordinated commands is exactly the failure Unified Command exists to prevent.

notes.front: A new responder is unsure how authority flows from the Incident Commander down through the organization. What ICS characteristic answers this?
notes.back: Chain of Command — the orderly line of authority within the organization.
notes.explanation: This is the general hierarchy question, distinct from Unity of Command’s single-supervisor rule.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: A responder receives conflicting task assignments from their ICS supervisor and their everyday department captain, who has come to help at the same incident. Whose direction should they follow?
notes.back: Their ICS supervisor only — Unity of Command means one designated supervisor at a time.
notes.explanation: This is the classic Unity of Command trap: a familiar day-to-day boss showing up at the same incident.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary
notes.choices:
A) Their ICS supervisor
B) Whichever instruction came first
C) Both, by splitting the task
notes.choicesExplained: B: order of arrival is irrelevant; the rule is about which role holds authority, not timing. C: splitting a task between two supervisors is exactly what Unity of Command exists to prevent.

notes.front: A resource is requested for an incident and works its shift, but its status changes are never recorded or reported. Which Accountability principle was skipped?
notes.back: Resource tracking — its status changes were never recorded or reported.
notes.explanation: This tests the end-to-end scope of Accountability, not just the check-in step.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 23, SM-p67

notes.front: A volunteer arrives at an incident and starts helping without reporting to anyone first. Have they completed Check-In?
notes.back: No — Check-In means reporting in to receive an assignment before working.
notes.explanation: This distinguishes simply being present from being formally checked in.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: A private crane operator hears about a landslide on the radio and drives to the scene without being called. What does the Dispatch/Deployment characteristic say about this?
notes.back: Resources not requested should refrain from self-dispatching, to avoid overburdening incident command.
notes.explanation: Self-dispatching, however well-meant, can overwhelm an incident that has not requested or accounted for the extra resource.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 24, SM-p68
notes.choices:
A) They should not self-dispatch; wait to be requested
B) They should go, since any help is useful
C) They should go, but only if their crane is well-maintained
notes.choicesExplained: B: unrequested arrivals can overwhelm command even if well-intentioned. C: equipment condition does not create an exception to the dispatch rule.

notes.front: A fire engine is formally ordered by the incident’s resource system to relocate to a new staging point. What is this movement called?
notes.back: Dispatch — an ordered movement to an assigned mission or between locations.
notes.explanation: This links the term to a specific, ordered (not self-initiated) movement.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: A Planning Section sets up a process to gather, verify and share updates on an evolving flood’s water levels. Which ICS characteristic is this?
notes.back: Information and Intelligence Management.
notes.explanation: This connects the definition to a concrete Planning Section activity.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 27, SM-p71

notes.front: A Public Information Officer gathers general situational updates from the field for a press briefing. Is this "intelligence" in the NIMS sense?
notes.back: No — NIMS "intelligence" refers exclusively to threat-related information from law enforcement, medical surveillance or investigative organizations.
notes.explanation: This tests the narrow, technical NIMS meaning against a broader everyday use of the word.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 2, Visual 27, SM-p71

notes.front: What is the difference between Unity of Command and Unified Command?
notes.back: Unity of Command: each person reports to one supervisor. Unified Command: several agencies jointly command one incident with shared objectives.
notes.explanation: Both are core NIMS terms with almost the same name; IS-200.c explicitly warns not to confuse them.
notes.contrast: Unity of Command is about an individual’s single reporting line; Unified Command is about several agencies sharing one command structure.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 1, Visual 3, SM-p34

notes.front: What is the difference between Plain Language and Clear Text?
notes.back: Plain Language: communication the audience understands, limiting jargon. Clear Text: communication that uses no codes at all.
notes.explanation: Clear Text is the stricter idea; Plain Language is the broader communication style it serves.
notes.contrast: Plain Language is about being understood; Clear Text is specifically about not using codes.
notes.source: https://training.fema.gov/programs/independent-study/_course-files/is-700.b/Handouts/National_Incident_Management%20System_Third%20Edition_October_2017.pdf#page=72

notes.front: What is the difference between Dispatch and the Dispatch/Deployment characteristic?
notes.back: Dispatch: the ordered movement of one resource to a mission. Dispatch/Deployment: the NIMS rule that resources move only when requested or dispatched.
notes.explanation: One names an action; the other is the governing rule that action must always follow.
notes.contrast: Dispatch is a specific movement; Dispatch/Deployment is the characteristic requiring that movement to be authorized.
notes.source: https://training.fema.gov/programs/independent-study/_course-files/is-700.b/Handouts/National_Incident_Management%20System_Third%20Edition_October_2017.pdf#page=73

notes.front: A wildfire is spreading into a second county’s jurisdiction and is expected to run for several more days. Should the team move to a written IAP now?
notes.back: Yes — growing complexity, multiple jurisdictions and runs past one operational period are exactly when a written IAP becomes increasingly important.
notes.explanation: This applies the rule to a concrete case combining two of its listed triggers at once.
notes.source: IS-0700.b Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 6, p71

notes.front: A police sergeant is assigned to an incident under a different ICS supervisor, but their everyday department captain also calls with instructions. Whose instructions apply on the incident?
notes.back: Only the ICS supervisor’s — once assigned, you no longer report to your day-to-day supervisor.
notes.explanation: This is the same day-to-day-supervisor trap applied to a fresh example.
